soil-phys-246.title: Greenhouse gases: the trace gases that warm the planet
soil-phys-246.text: Without greenhouse gases, Earth's average surface temperature would be about -18 °C instead of the present 15 °C. A greenhouse gas is a gas in an atmosphere that absorbs the heat a planet radiates and so raises its surface temperature. Nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of dry air, barely absorb infrared. Carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide and other trace gases, under 0.1% of the atmosphere, absorb it because their molecules are asymmetric in charge. Water vapor causes 41-67% of the greenhouse effect, but its short residence time of about nine days means human activity barely changes it globally; it amplifies warming through water vapor feedback. Concentrations follow the balance of sources and sinks. Soil, oceans and vegetation are sinks, and about 0.55 of emitted CO2 is absorbed by land and ocean sinks in the first year. Most human CO2 comes from fossil fuels. Agriculture is a major methane source, with rice paddies giving 22% of agricultural methane and 11% of nitrous oxide.

soil-phys-159.title: Needle ice: frost columns that heave seedlings from the ground
soil-phys-159.text:
On a cold night, columns of ice can grow straight up out of bare soil. Needle ice is needle-shaped columns of ice that grow from groundwater at the soil surface. It forms when the soil is above 0 °C but the air at the surface is below 0 °C: water rises by capillary action and freezes onto the growing column. Needles are typically a few centimeters long. Ten centimeters is the recorded maximum, though specimens of 15-20 cm have been seen at Gerðuberg.

It needs ice segregation, in which supercooled water freezes onto existing ice in a porous medium, and it favors soils high in silt and organic matter. It is {{ref:soil-phys-153}} at the start of the freezing season, before there is any soil overburden to lift. Taber found that pore size controls the amount of frost heave, and that a gradient of soil moisture tension drives water up toward the freezing front near the surface.

Growing needles lift soil particles and crusts, which settle unevenly on melting. They disturb streambanks, aid soil creep and shape patterned ground. They also heave seedlings out of the ground, and the seedlings often die because they do not resettle or their roots dry out. Swedish pipkrake, coined in 1907 by Henrik Hesselman, is one of several names. Others are frost pillars, Kammeis and shimobashira. See {{ref:soil-phys-137}} for the soil temperatures involved.

soil-phys-240.title: Diffusion: spreading over short distances
soil-phys-240.text:
Diffusion does its work over tiny distances. Under normal conditions molecular diffusion dominates only over lengths from nanometers to millimeters; beyond that, convection takes over. It is the net movement of atoms, ions, molecules or energy from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration. A gradient in chemical potential drives it, which sets it apart from bulk flow, where a whole body of material moves down a pressure gradient.

{{ref:soil-phys-181}} puts numbers on it. The diffusive flux is proportional to the negative concentration gradient, with the diffusion coefficient D as the constant. In a porous medium such as soil, the porosity must be counted in both the flux and accumulation terms. As porosity goes to zero, the molar flux for a given concentration gradient goes to zero too.

soil-phys-244.title: Partial pressure: each gas in a mixture on its own
soil-phys-244.text: In a mixture of gases, each gas acts as if it were alone. Partial pressure is the pressure a single gas in a mixture would exert if it alone filled the whole volume at the same temperature. By Dalton's law, the total pressure of an ideal gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its gases. The partial pressure of a component equals its mole fraction times the total pressure, and its mole fraction equals its volume fraction. Gases dissolve, diffuse and react according to their partial pressures, not their concentrations, which links it to {{ref:soil-phys-240}}. For non-ideal gases the concept generalizes to fugacity.

soil-phys-243.title: Molecular diffusion: the restless motion that mixes gases and liquids
soil-phys-243.text: Above absolute zero, molecules never sit still. Molecular diffusion is the motion of atoms, molecules or other particles of a gas or liquid at temperatures above absolute zero, which spreads them from high to low concentration, as in {{ref:soil-phys-240}}. The rate depends on temperature, fluid viscosity and particle size and mass. The result is gradual mixing until the distribution is uniform. After that, molecules keep moving in a dynamic equilibrium. Chemical diffusion needs a gradient; self-diffusion does not. For gases, {{ref:soil-phys-181}} gives the rate as proportional to the concentration gradient, where there is no bulk motion. Molecular diffusion is one of the slower mass-transport mechanisms.

soil-phys-242.title: Heat capacity: how much heat it takes to warm something
soil-phys-242.text: How much heat does it take to warm an object? Heat capacity is the answer: the amount of heat that must be supplied to an object to raise its temperature by one unit. The SI unit is joule per kelvin. Dividing by mass gives specific heat capacity, and dividing by volume gives volumetric heat capacity. It varies with starting temperature and pressure, and changes sharply at phase transitions such as melting or vaporization. The heat capacity of a heterogeneous object can usually be found by adding the capacities of its parts.

soil-phys-245.title: Thermal conductivity: how readily a material passes heat
soil-phys-245.text: Ice conducts heat far better than liquid water: 2.18 W/(m·K) at 0 °C against 0.56. Thermal conductivity is a measure of a material's intrinsic ability to conduct heat locally, in watts per meter-kelvin. Conduction is energy transport by random molecular motion across a temperature gradient, without macroscopic flows, and heat flows from high to low temperature. Heat capacity ({{ref:soil-phys-242}}) says how much heat a material takes up; conductivity says how readily it passes heat along. Methods of measuring are steady-state, which wait for a steady temperature profile, or transient, which use the system as it approaches steady state. Without convection, air and other gases are good insulators, so insulating materials work by trapping many gas-filled pockets that block conduction. Conductivity can differ with direction: wood conducts better along the grain than across it.

soil-phys-247.title: Global warming potential: comparing gases against carbon dioxide
soil-phys-247.text: A tonne of methane leaked equals 81.2 tonnes of CO2 over 20 years. Global warming potential, or GWP, is a dimensionless measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a chosen period, as a multiple of the warming from the same mass of CO2. CO2 has a GWP of 1 by definition. For other gases it depends on how strongly the gas absorbs thermal radiation, how fast it leaves the atmosphere and the time frame. Methane's 20-year GWP is 81.2.

soil-phys-248.title: Growing regions: where climate and soil favor a crop
soil-phys-248.text: Some regions are known by a single crop. A growing region is a geographic area whose climate, soil and farming practices favor producing particular crops, plants or livestock. A region may be dominated by one crop, such as the American Corn Belt, or be diverse where soil fertility and seasonal rainfall are high, as in Queensland and New South Wales. Cultivation may be enabled by a regional climate or a unique microclimate, and regions are often aligned along a latitude because crops need consistent climate.

soil-phys-241.title: The diffusion equation: one law for spreading heat and solutes
soil-phys-241.text: One equation describes how a diffusing material spreads in space and time. The diffusion equation is a parabolic partial differential equation that describes how the density of a diffusing material changes in space and time. It follows from the continuity equation ({{ref:soil-phys-255}}), which says material is neither created nor destroyed, combined with {{ref:soil-phys-181}}. With a constant diffusion coefficient it is linear and identical to the {{ref:soil-phys-183}}; if the coefficient depends on density it is nonlinear. It is the special case of the {{ref:soil-phys-197}} in which bulk velocity is zero.

soil-chem-231.title: Anatase: the short-lived form of titanium dioxide
soil-chem-231.text: Titanium dioxide comes in several forms, and anatase is the one that does not last. Anatase is a metastable tetragonal mineral form of titanium dioxide (TiO2), one of the oxide minerals of {{ref:soil-found-035}}. Rutile is the most common and stable polymorph. Anatase is metastable at all temperatures and pressures but often forms first because of its lower surface energy. It forms at relatively low temperatures. It occurs in minor amounts in {{ref:soil-form-135}} and {{ref:soil-form-137}}, and as microscopic crystals in sandstones, clays and slates. It converts to rutile between 550 and about 1000 degrees C, depending on impurities and sample morphology. It is also less dense than rutile, about 3.9 against 4.2.

soil-chem-238.title: How clay minerals differ in charge and surface area
soil-chem-238.text: Clay minerals of one family can differ enormously in how much they hold. Phyllosilicates differ mainly in cation exchange capacity, CEC, and in reactive surface area, which depend on isomorphous substitution and on whether the interlayer admits cations. Kaolinite has little substitution and does not expand, so its CEC is 2-16 cmol(+) per kg and its surface is only external, 5-15 m2 per g. Illite and chlorite have substantial substitution, but a tightly bound K+ or hydroxide interlayer blocks expansion, so CEC is limited: 20-40 for illite and 10-40 for chlorite. Smectite admits interlayer cations, giving CEC 60-120 and an internal surface of 570-660 m2 per g, and soils rich in it swell and shrink strongly. Vermiculite has CEC of 100-150 but expands little, because its charge, concentrated near the interlayer, binds cations tightly and restricts water entry. Fe/Al oxyhydroxides have CEC near 0-3 but 200-500 m2 per g of surface, and amorphous aluminosilicates range from 5 to 350 CEC.

soil-chem-237.title: Quartz, the mineral that fills the sand
soil-chem-237.text: Quartz (alpha-SiO2) is the most common mineral in Canadian soils, and it makes up about 40-60% of the sand fraction. It is a framework silicate ({{ref:soil-found-031}}) in which every silica tetrahedron shares all four oxygens. It is essentially pure SiO2 and needs no other bonding ions. Strong Si-O covalent bonds make its solubility very low and its dissolution extremely slow, so quartz accumulates over time, for example in Ae horizons of Podzolic and Luvisolic soils. It is also a major part of the silt and a small part of the clay fraction.

soil-chem-235.title: Secondary minerals: what weathering builds from the wreckage
soil-chem-235.text: Weathering makes new minerals as well as breaking down old ones. A secondary mineral is a by-product of chemical weathering, formed by partial alteration of a primary mineral ({{ref:soil-form-140}}) or by precipitation from components dissolved from other minerals. Primary minerals form as the original molten crust cools and solidifies, while secondary minerals form from their breakdown products. In heavily weathered soils secondary minerals dominate, including iron and aluminum oxides from primary igneous silicates. Most are hydrated aluminosilicates (phyllosilicates, or clay minerals) or Fe and Al oxyhydroxides, which are stable in soils. Clay minerals are the most chemically reactive inorganic phases in soil; their amount and type influence porosity, swelling, compressibility, sorption and exchange capacity, and hydraulic conductivity. In glaciated Canada most secondary minerals formed before the last glaciation and were redeposited, so little has formed since compared with the amount inherited.
